ACTIONS CACHE POISONING CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Can a fork PR poison your GitHub Actions cache?

Actions cache entries are scoped to the whole repository, not to a branch or a trust level. A job triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run runs with your secrets even though a stranger's fork raised the event — and if it writes to actions/cache, that stranger controls what a later, privileged workflow may restore. This is the exact root cause of the TanStack Router incident (May 2026). Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds both a fork-writable cache and a restore-keys fallback that can adopt a colliding entry, each with the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeDetailFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added finding before it merges.

Common questions

What is GitHub Actions cache poisoning?

GitHub Actions cache entries are scoped to the repository, not to the branch or the trust level of whoever triggered the run that wrote them. If a job triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run — which runs with the base repository's secrets even though a stranger's fork raised the event — writes to the cache, the fork controls what a later, more privileged workflow may restore. In the TanStack Router incident (May 2026), a fork PR wrote a poisoned dependency-store cache entry on every push, and the project's release pipeline later restored and executed it.

What does restore-keys have to do with it?

restore-keys is a fallback list: a miss on the exact cache key can still restore a different entry that only shares the key prefix. Independent researchers (AdnaneKhan's ActionsCacheBlasting proof-of-concept, Hive Security's cache-poisoning writeup) describe this in practice as "all keys are restore keys" — an attacker who can write any entry under a shared prefix, including from an unrelated unprivileged job, can get a privileged restore-keys fallback to adopt it on the next miss.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste your workflow YAML and the scan runs entirely in this page.

Does a clean scan mean my cache usage is safe?

No. This checks two specific, well-documented patterns in a single workflow file at a time. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your repository's overall security. It does not catch the cache: input on actions/setup-node, actions/setup-python, actions/setup-java, or actions/setup-go, and it does not correlate a cache write in one workflow file with a restore in another.

Why is unscoped restore-keys flagged regardless of trigger type?

The risk lives on the restoring side, not the triggering side: a restore-keys fallback is exactly as adoptable on a push-to-main workflow as anywhere else, if anything in the repository — including an unrelated, unprivileged job — can write a cache entry under the same key prefix.

More: what is GitHub Actions cache poisoning? · how this differs from zizmor's cache-poisoning audit · where a manual read holds up and where it slips

vs-checking-by-hand.html.text:
← Actions Cache Poisoning Check

Actions Cache Poisoning Check vs. reviewing workflows by eye

Reading a workflow file for these two patterns is a real skill, and an experienced reviewer catches the obvious case every time. This page names no product or company -- "reviewing by eye" is the generic habit every maintainer already has, not a competing tool.

Where a careful read holds up, and where it slips

A bare actions/cache step sitting right below a pull_request_target: trigger is easy to spot once you know the shape. Two things are harder to hold in your head while scanning a real workflow file: actions/cache has three call shapes -- bare (reads and writes), /save (writes only), and /restore (reads only) -- and only the first two can actually poison anything, so a rule that flags every actions/cache string either raises a false alarm on a read-only restore or, worse, gets tuned so loosely a real write-capable step slips past. And restore-keys risk is not about the trigger at all: it depends on whether anything else in the repository can write an entry under the same key prefix, which means the natural instinct -- filter for pull_request_target or workflow_run first, then look inside -- skips over every ordinary push workflow's cache step, which is exactly where a prefix collision is adopted.

Where to answer each question.
CaseReviewing by eyeThis tool
Bare actions/cache step under a pull_request_target triggerEasy to catchCatches it the same way
actions/cache/restore step under the same triggerEasy to flag by mistake -- it only reads, so it cannot write a poisoned entryParses the step variant and applies the write-capable rule only to bare and /save
actions/cache/save step under a fork triggerEasy to skim past assuming "save" sounds routine, unlike a bare cache stepTreated the same as a bare step -- both write
restore-keys on a workflow triggered by pull_request_target/workflow_runCaught, since the reviewer is already looking at this file for fork-trigger riskCaught the same way
restore-keys on an ordinary push-to-main workflowEasy to skip entirely -- nothing about the trigger looks untrusted, so the file doesn't get a second lookFlagged regardless of trigger, since the risk depends on who else can write the shared key prefix, not on what triggered the restore
A repository with a dozen workflow files, each with its own cache stepRe-reading all of them for both patterns, every time a workflow changes, is tedious and easy to shortcutPaste as many files as you have, or run check.py across the whole directory
Blocking a newly-added finding before it mergesDepends on a human noticing it in reviewcheck.py --fail-on-risk gives a real exit code from the same classification, wired into your own CI

The two are complementary, not competing: this tool does not replace the judgment that decides whether a flagged cache step is actually reachable from an attacker in your specific setup -- it replaces the tedious, error-prone part, which is remembering which cache-action variant writes and checking every file's restore-keys regardless of what triggered it.

Run the free cache poisoning check

Common questions

What does reviewing a workflow for cache poisoning by eye actually catch?

A reviewer who knows the pattern will catch the obvious case: a pull_request_target or workflow_run workflow with a bare actions/cache step a few lines below the trigger. That recognition is real, and this tool checks the same two conditions -- an untrusted trigger and a cache-writing step -- rather than a wider or different rule.

Why is the save/restore variant distinction easy to get wrong by eye?

actions/cache/restore only reads -- it cannot write a poisoned entry no matter what triggered the job, so flagging it would be a false alarm. A bare actions/cache or actions/cache/save step does write. A reviewer scanning quickly for the string actions/cache under a fork trigger can easily flag the restore-only step as risky, or worse, skim past a bare actions/cache step assuming it only reads because a nearby step in the same job happens to say "restore" in a comment or variable name. This tool parses the actual step reference -- actions/cache, actions/cache/save, or actions/cache/restore -- and applies the write-capable rule only to the first two.

Why is unscoped restore-keys easy to miss even on an ordinary push workflow?

The instinct when hunting for cache poisoning is to search for pull_request_target or workflow_run first, then look at what's inside. But restore-keys risk has nothing to do with which trigger fired the job doing the restoring -- it depends on whether anything else in the repository, including an unrelated and unprivileged job, can write a cache entry under the same key prefix. A reviewer who filters by trigger first will skip every ordinary push or pull_request workflow's cache step without a second look, which is exactly where an adopted prefix collision shows up. This tool flags restore-keys on any cache step regardless of trigger, because the risk lives on the restoring side, not the triggering side.

Does a clean result from this tool mean my cache usage is safe?

No. It checks two specific, well-documented patterns in one workflow file at a time. It does not catch the cache: input on actions/setup-node, actions/setup-python, actions/setup-java, or actions/setup-go, and it does not correlate a cache write in one workflow file with a restore in another -- both real ways a repository's cache usage can still be exploitable after a clean scan.

vs-zizmor.html.text:
← Actions Cache Poisoning Check

GitHub Actions Cache Poisoning Check vs. zizmor

Both name the same risk and check different sides of it. zizmor's cache-poisoning audit looks at whether a release job is trusting a cache it should not. This tool looks at whether a fork can write that cache in the first place, and whether restore-keys can adopt a poisoned entry -- in any workflow, free, in your browser, with nothing to install.

What each tool is for

zizmor (github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis tool for GitHub Actions, installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor and run against workflow files or a whole repository. Its cache-poisoning audit, per its own documentation, detects potential cache-poisoning scenarios in release workflows: it identifies a job as a release or publish step by its trigger (a tag push, a release event) or by its use of a known publisher action (pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish, softprops/action-gh-release, and similar), and flags one that also has a cache-aware action enabled -- actions/cache and roughly two dozen others, including framework-specific ones such as actions/setup-node and Swatinem/rust-cache -- on the reasoning that a release pipeline should not restore a cache an earlier, less-trusted run may have written.

This checker looks at the other side of the same risk, in any workflow rather than only release ones: you paste the YAML of a workflow file, and it lists every actions/cache or actions/cache/save write step reachable from a pull_request_target or workflow_run trigger -- where a fork's pull request controls what gets written -- and every restore-keys fallback with no explicit scope, which can adopt a colliding entry written by an unrelated, unprivileged job. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no install and no token, and makes no network call of its own under any configuration.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to know whether a release/publish job in my repo is trusting a cache an earlier, less-trusted run could have written.zizmor's cache-poisoning audit -- that is exactly the scenario it targets.
I want to know whether a pull_request_target or workflow_run job in my repo can write to the Actions cache.This checker -- zizmor's audit does not check who wrote a cache entry, only whether one is active in a job it identifies as a release step.
I want to know whether my restore-keys fallback can adopt an entry a different, unprivileged job wrote.This checker -- restore-keys is outside the scope of zizmor's cache-poisoning audit entirely.
I want one maintained scanner covering dozens of GitHub Actions security patterns beyond caching -- permissions, credential leakage, injection, impostor commits, and more.zizmor -- that breadth is its whole job; this tool checks only the two cache patterns above.
I don't want to install a CLI (pip or cargo) or add a new GitHub Action just to check one file.This checker -- it is a page, not a package.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run zizmor in CI for the release-workflow question and still reach for this tool the moment the question is the write side or restore-keys, which zizmor's cache-poisoning audit does not check.

Run the free cache poisoning check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or zizmor's cache-poisoning audit?

They both name GitHub Actions cache poisoning but check different sides of it. zizmor is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis CLI (installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor) whose cache-poisoning audit, per its own documentation, detects potential cache-poisoning scenarios in release workflows -- it looks at jobs it recognises as publishing a release (a tag-push or release trigger, or a known publisher action such as pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish or softprops/action-gh-release) and flags one still using a cache-aware action there, on the reasoning that a release pipeline should not trust a cache an earlier, less-trusted run could have written. This checker looks at the other side of the same risk, in any workflow, not only release ones: an actions/cache or actions/cache/save write step reachable from a pull_request_target or workflow_run trigger -- where a fork controls what gets written -- and an unscoped restore-keys fallback that can adopt a colliding entry regardless of who wrote it. Run zizmor for the release-workflow question; paste a file here for the write-side and restore-keys questions.

Does zizmor's cache-poisoning audit already catch what this tool catches?

Not the same ground. zizmor's audit is scoped to release workflows specifically and, per its published source, does not inspect restore-keys at all -- it checks whether a cache-aware action (actions/cache and roughly two dozen others, including framework-specific ones like actions/setup-node and Swatinem/rust-cache) is active in a job it has identified as a publish step, and suggests turning caching off there. This tool's two findings -- a cache write reachable from pull_request_target/workflow_run, and an unscoped restore-keys fallback -- are not the release-workflow question zizmor asks, so a clean zizmor run on a repository can still carry either of this tool's findings, and a clean scan here says nothing about whether a release job is needlessly trusting a cache.

Why use a narrower tool if zizmor already covers more ground?

Two reasons. First, zizmor is a CLI you install and point at files or a repository; this tool is a page you paste a workflow into, with nothing to install, which is faster when you want an answer on the one file in front of you. Second, and more to the point, the two catch genuinely different patterns rather than one being a subset of the other: zizmor's audit does not look at restore-keys or at which trigger wrote a cache entry, so a repository can pass its release-workflow check and still have a fork-writable cache or an unscoped restore-keys fallback that this tool exists to name.

Does this tool need a GitHub token the way zizmor sometimes does?

No, never. zizmor documents an optional online mode -- set GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN -- for audits that benefit from GitHub API access, and runs offline by default otherwise, which already covers its cache-poisoning audit. This tool has no online mode to opt into: nothing here talks to a server under any configuration, so there is no token to supply.

Is this page affiliated with zizmor or its maintainers?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by zizmor, zizmorcore, or its maintainers. zizmor is an independent open-source project, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation and source at github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor and docs.zizmor.sh.

what-is-github-actions-cache-poisoning.h.text:
← Actions Cache Poisoning Check

What is GitHub Actions cache poisoning?

GitHub Actions caches are scoped to the whole repository, not to a branch, a workflow, or a trust level. pull_request, the ordinary PR trigger, runs with a read-only token and no secrets — a cache it writes is not especially dangerous, because nothing valuable trusts it either. pull_request_target and workflow_run exist for jobs that need more: commenting on a PR, or building it with real credentials. They run in the context of the base repository, with the base repository's secrets — but the event that triggers them is still raised by whoever opened the pull request, who might be a stranger.

If a job on one of those two triggers writes to the cache, the stranger controls what gets written:

on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.pnpm-store
          key: pnpm-${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: pnpm install

actions/cache restores on a hit and saves on a miss, so this step writes a cache entry the fork PR fully controls the contents of. If a separate, privileged workflow — a release build, a deploy step, anything triggered by a push to a protected branch — later restores from the same key namespace, it can pick up the fork's poisoned entry and run it with real secrets.

A real incident

In May 2026, a pull request opened against TanStack Router's pull_request_target workflow wrote a poisoned pnpm store to the shared Actions cache on every push. The project's own release pipeline later restored that cache and executed the payload. Independent security researchers (AdnaneKhan's ActionsCacheBlasting proof-of-concept, Hive Security's cache-poisoning writeup) had already documented the underlying mechanism: caches are not segregated by workflow, event type, or trust level, and a restore-keys fallback can adopt an entry that merely shares a key prefix with the one you actually asked for — described as "all keys are restore keys" in practice.

The fix

  • Do not write to the cache from a job reachable by pull_request_target or workflow_run. If the job genuinely needs to build the fork's code, keep that build unprivileged (plain pull_request) and hand off only reviewed results as artifacts to the privileged job.
  • If a fork-triggered job must cache something, key it so no privileged job ever restores from the same namespace — prefix the key with the untrusted run's own run ID, never a branch name or a lockfile hash a privileged job also uses.
  • Narrow or drop restore-keys fallback lists, especially on a cache a privileged workflow trusts. An exact-key miss that falls through to "anything with this prefix" is exactly the mechanism a poisoned entry rides in on.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions Cache Poisoning Check to find every fork-writable cache step and unscoped restore-keys fallback across every workflow file at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any workflow has either pattern — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added one before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean a workflow is safe — only that these two documented patterns were not found.
